definitions.content: At a neighborhood workshop, Lina placed a box of spare pencils beside the door. Visitors could take one and leave another when they had a spare. definitions.title: The focus trick
definitions.claim: A study club posts, “Our five-minute reset makes almost everyone concentrate better.”

evidence.title: The poll
evidence.body: Nine of the ten volunteers said they felt more focused immediately afterwards.

evidence.title: The method
evidence.body: Everyone tried the reset. Nobody was asked to do a different activity, and there was no concentration test.

evidence.title: The audience
evidence.body: Volunteers were members of one after-school study club. More than 300 students follow the account.

questions.prompt: Which statement reflects what was recorded?
options: Nine students passed a focus test
Nine volunteers reported feeling more focused
questions.explanation: The poll recorded nine self-reports. It did not measure test performance or ask the followers.

questions.prompt: What does 90% describe here?
options: The share of the ten volunteers
questions.explanation: Nine out of the ten people who responded is 90%. The denominator is ten.

questions.prompt: Which piece of evidence would best help test whether the reset itself caused a change?
options: A comparable group that did a different activity
questions.explanation: A comparison group helps separate the reset from other causes, such as expectations or a quiet room.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite is justified?
options: Followers who saw the post improved
Most of the volunteers said they felt more focused that day
questions.explanation: This wording preserves who answered, what they reported, and when.

definitions.claim: A shared screenshot says the library now stays open late every evening.

evidence.title: Library notice

questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses a preference?
options: The new hours are the best
The flyer was for exam week
questions.explanation: “Best” expresses the reader’s judgment. The other statements are checkable details.

questions.prompt: Which evidence should you use for next Thursday?
questions.explanation: The official current notice directly lists Thursday’s hours.

questions.prompt: Why does the old flyer fail to support the screenshot?
options: The flyer covers a different period
questions.explanation: The 21:00 time was for an exam week that has ended.

evidence.title: Tuesday log
evidence.body: The bus left at 08:00 and arrived at 08:22.

evidence.title: Tuesday log
evidence.body: The bus left at 08:00 and arrived at 08:28.

evidence.title: Friday log
evidence.body: At 08:00, River took 31 minutes and Park took 25 minutes.

questions.prompt: Which route was faster on Tuesday?
options: The logs omit the start times
questions.explanation: River took 22 minutes and Park took 28.

questions.prompt: Which entry directly challenges the word “always”?
questions.explanation: On Friday, Park was six minutes quicker than River.

questions.prompt: What is the most accurate summary of the logs?
options: River was faster Tuesday and Park was faster Friday
questions.explanation: The logs show a different quicker route on each of the two observed days.

questions.prompt: What would improve an estimate for future trips?
options: Comparing logs over more comparable days and times
questions.explanation: More trips at comparable times give better evidence of how the routes usually perform.

definitions.title: Half the waste?
definitions.claim: A café shares, “Reusable cups cut our monthly waste in half.”

evidence.title: April record
evidence.body: The café discarded 100 single-use cups in April.

evidence.title: May record
evidence.body: The café introduced reusable cups and discarded 50 single-use cups in May.

evidence.title: Reporting note
evidence.body: Staff counted cups only. They did not count packaging, spoiled food, or other rubbish.

questions.prompt: Which number was halved?
options: The share of drinks in disposable cups
questions.explanation: Cup count fell from 100 to 50. Total rubbish was not measured.

questions.prompt: How did discarded cups per drink change?
questions.explanation: 100 of 200 and 50 of 100 are both one cup for every two drinks.

questions.prompt: What should the café collect to support a claim about total waste?
options: The same measure of all waste categories in both periods
A review of the drink menu
questions.explanation: The claim covers all waste, so it needs comparable measurements of all waste categories.

questions.prompt: Which headline fits the evidence?
options: Half the customers stopped using cups
Fewer cups were discarded as drink sales also fell
questions.explanation: The records show count changes but do not show a lower per-drink rate or establish cause.

definitions.title: The quiet seats test
definitions.claim: A campus post says, “The north room makes people work for longer.”

evidence.title: Room log
evidence.body: Median stay was 42 minutes. Visitors were mainly on study breaks between lectures.

evidence.title: Room log
evidence.body: Median stay was 29 minutes. Most visitors came while waiting for a shuttle every 30 minutes.

evidence.title: Observer’s note
evidence.body: The observer noted arrival and departure. They did not track what anyone did inside.

questions.prompt: What was measured directly?
questions.explanation: The observer recorded entry and exit, which allows duration to be calculated.

questions.prompt: What plausible explanation besides the room itself fits the result?
options: South visitors often left to meet shuttle times
Both rooms had the same number of visitors
questions.explanation: Different reasons for visiting can change when people leave, even if rooms have the same effect.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is supported?
options: The observed median stay was longer in the north room
questions.explanation: 42 minutes exceeds 29. A difference in medians does not prove every stay differed or establish cause.

questions.prompt: Which change would best test the claim about work?
options: Assign similar participants to rooms at random and measure work time consistently
Ask which room has nicer walls
questions.explanation: Comparable groups and a measure of actual work address both confounding and measurement.

definitions.claim: A neighborhood chat shares a pool-closure screenshot with the caption “Closed today.”

evidence.title: Image
evidence.body: The notice in the image says “Closed Friday for pump maintenance.” It does not show a date.

evidence.title: Official update
evidence.body: The pool’s posted schedule lists normal Friday hours for this week.

evidence.title: Archived notice
evidence.body: A dated pool notice has the exact maintenance wording shown in the cropped image.

questions.prompt: What essential detail is missing from the screenshot?
questions.explanation: Friday occurs every week. A date is needed to connect the notice to this week.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most directly addresses this week?
options: The number of people who forwarded it
questions.explanation: The official update explicitly applies to the current week.

questions.prompt: What does the archive add to the investigation?
options: The same wording was used in a dated notice four weeks earlier
questions.explanation: The matching earlier notice gives a plausible source for the undated image.

questions.prompt: What is the most accurate reply?
options: It is definitely closed every Friday
The old notice proves that every future change is false
The current schedule shows normal hours. The screenshot may be from an earlier closure.
questions.explanation: The dated sources support the current schedule and explain the older wording while leaving room for a later update.

definitions.title: The homework reminder trial
definitions.claim: A newsletter credits message reminders for “better completion in all groups.”

evidence.title: Reminder group
evidence.body: Experienced students: 72 of 80 completed. New students: 8 of 20 completed.

evidence.title: No-reminder group
evidence.body: Experienced students: 19 of 20 completed. New students: 41 of 80 completed.

evidence.title: Assignment note
evidence.body: The study team did not randomly assign people. “Experienced” meant having finished a previous course.

questions.prompt: Which group had the higher overall completion rate?
questions.explanation: The overall rates were 80% and 60%, respectively.

questions.prompt: Within each experience group, which group had the higher observed completion rate?
questions.explanation: Experienced: 95% without reminders versus 90% with them. New: about 51% without versus 40% with.

questions.prompt: What helps explain why the overall comparison goes the other way?
options: The outcomes were recorded in hours
Experienced students made up a larger share of the reminder group
questions.explanation: Experienced students finished more often in both groups and formed 80% of the reminder group but only 20% of the comparison group.

questions.prompt: Which decision best follows from these records?
options: Use a better controlled trial before attributing a benefit to reminders
Stop all reminders because they are proven harmful
questions.explanation: Selection and different group composition prevent either direction of the observed association from proving a causal effect.

definitions.title: The battery test
definitions.claim: An app comparison headline says that Lite mode saves battery on every phone.

evidence.title: SmallPhone lab
evidence.body: With the same device and brightness, Lite fell 8 points per hour and Standard fell 12 on the same video.

evidence.title: LargePhone lab
evidence.body: Lite fell 10 points and Standard fell 9 on the same video. Conditions were held fixed for this device.

evidence.title: Third review
evidence.body: A reviewer ended the day at 60% with Lite and 40% with Standard. The two days had different screen time.

questions.prompt: How much smaller was the drop on SmallPhone in Lite mode?
options: Two percent of the remaining battery
questions.explanation: The per-hour drops were 12 and 8 points. Their difference is four points.

questions.prompt: Which source offers a direct counterexample to “every phone”?
questions.explanation: Lite used one more point per hour on that device under its matched conditions.

questions.prompt: Why can the end-of-day reviewer’s numbers fail to isolate the effect?
options: The device could not have a battery
Screen time differed between the two days
questions.explanation: More or less screen time changes battery use independent of the app mode.

questions.prompt: What is a justified takeaway for a third phone model?
options: Lite is guaranteed to save four points
The comparison must be tested under comparable conditions on that model
The uncontrolled review settles the result
questions.explanation: Two models behaved differently. A matched test on the third model would be relevant evidence.

definitions.title: The reading app’s cohort
definitions.claim: A fictional app claims, “Using the app makes readers finish twice as many articles.”

evidence.title: Dashboard
evidence.body: The dashboard compares the per-person median for users who returned daily with the median for visitors who opened the app only once.

evidence.title: Counting rule
evidence.body: Both groups used the same definition of “finish,” but the dashboard includes articles opened only in the app.

evidence.title: Follow-up
evidence.body: A poll found daily returners already reported reading more often before joining. No before-and-after totals were collected.

questions.prompt: What comparison did the dashboard actually make?
options: Before and after for each reader
Typical finishes among daily returners versus one-time visitors
App versus no app in a randomized trial
questions.explanation: The comparison was between distinct groups defined by how often they opened the app.

questions.prompt: What alternative explanation fits the follow-up?
options: The amount of reading was experimentally fixed
The two groups contained the same people
People who already read often may be more likely to return
The app must have changed reading outside it
questions.explanation: The groups may differ before exposure, so the comparison mixes prior habits with possible app effects.

questions.prompt: What would be needed to claim an effect on overall reading?
options: Comparable groups and a common measure that covers reading both inside and outside the app
More app-only charts for the same users
questions.explanation: App-only finishes miss reading elsewhere, and comparable groups help distinguish initial differences from an effect.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion best summarizes the evidence?
options: The app doubles reading for all users
Daily returners finished more articles in the app during the measured week
questions.explanation: The descriptive comparison is supported. It cannot identify a change caused by the app.
